How Leaves Capture Light

By A. Botanist

Every green leaf is a solar panel that builds itself. Inside its cells, thousands of chloroplasts collect sunlight and use it to split water, releasing the oxygen we breathe and storing energy in chemical bonds.

Pigments do the catching

Chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b absorb red and blue light strongly but reflect green light, which is why leaves look green to us. Accessory pigments called carotenoids widen the range of usable light and protect the cell from damage when the light is too intense.

A single leaf can hold more than a million chloroplasts in one square millimetre.

The light reactions step by step

  1. Photons excite electrons in photosystem II.
  2. Water is split to replace those electrons, and oxygen is released.
  3. Excited electrons travel along a transport chain that pumps protons.
  4. Photosystem I re-energizes the electrons, which reduce NADP+ to NADPH.
  5. The proton gradient drives ATP synthase, which makes ATP.

Why it matters

The ATP and NADPH made here power the Calvin cycle, which fixes carbon dioxide into sugar. Without the light reactions there would be no food chain on land and almost no oxygen in the atmosphere. Read more in the Calvin cycle primer.

  • Light reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes.
  • The Calvin cycle happens in the stroma.
  • Both stages are needed to build glucose.

Scientists still study how plants balance light capture against damage, because better control could raise crop yields in a warming climate.
